title: A Classroom Management Secret You've Never Heard Of r-heard/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin's short weekly post names a 'secret' of classroom management that rarely gets discussed: high competence. He means excellence across everything within a teacher's control, including schedule, organization, preparation, presentation, consistency, clarity, order, detail, precision, simplicity, neatness and personal dress. His claim is that children are impressed by competent adults because competence is rare in schools, and that when students see a teacher who is so reliably in command they relax, trust the leader and drop the urge to disrupt. He is clear that this sits on top of a management plan followed 'to a tee', with nonnegotiable rules and consistently enforced consequences. Linsin reduces the whole thing to one trait, discipline, on the grounds that how you do anything is how you do everything. The promised result is that good behavior, politeness and a drive for excellence appear naturally once students are convinced the teacher is exceptional every day.
points: Linsin's 'secret' is high competence: excellence in the many controllable parts of running a classroom, from schedule and preparation to neatness and personal dress.
Students trust and relax around a visibly competent leader, which lowers their anxieties and the temptation to misbehave.
Competence does not replace a classroom management plan; rules must stay clear and nonnegotiable and consequences enforced consistently.
The underlying trait is discipline, since you either are organized and neat or you are not.
Behavior, politeness and student drive follow naturally from daily, sustained excellence rather than from tactics alone.
quotes: This secret effortlessly draws students to their work and the challenges you place before them rather than the temptations of misbehavior.
The idea is to be so good at these controllables that students know beyond any doubt that they’re in safe hands.
People in general and kids in particular are impressed by highly competent people. The reason is because it’s rare, especially on a school campus.
This signals to students that they can trust their teacher implicitly. A true leader is in charge. Therefore, they can let down their guard.
Of course, you still must have a classroom management plan you follow to a tee. Your rules must be clear and nonnegotiable. Your consequences enforced like an NFL referee.
In reality, however, you only need one trait: discipline. Because you don’t work on being organized, for example, or work on being neatly dressed. You either are or you aren’t.
Simply prove to your students that you’re a highly competent leader and it all happens naturally.
